introduction: The study aimed to analyze depression and physical activity among employees seeking support from a digital mental health platform, examine their baseline association, and investigate changes over time. The authors note a paucity of data on the impact of a multi-modal digital mental health platform like this on different areas of health and well-being.
methodology: Prospective, observational study of adults with access to an employer-sponsored, multi-modal digital mental health benefits platform (Modern Health, San Francisco, CA). Conducted September 2021 to May 2022 in the United States. Participants completed an online baseline survey and a follow-up survey three months later, using the IPAQ-Short Form and the PHQ-9 on Qualtrics. Analyses were run in R, with paired t-tests and Spearman rank correlations.
results: Of 755 adults at baseline, 47.3% (n = 357) were underactive. Men averaged 49 more MVPA minutes per week than women. Underactive participants (n = 211) increased MVPA by 60.33 min/week (117%), and 27.5% became active. Among those with a positive screen (n = 178), PHQ-9 fell by 4.88 points, and 66.9% improved or recovered. Active participants reported no statistically significant change in activity.
discussion: The authors state that digital mental health platforms can support both symptom improvement and maintenance of positive mental health outcomes, and that digital, remotely delivered interventions may be particularly beneficial for underactive adults. They suggest that employer-sponsored platforms offering integrated mental and physical health resources may create a more supportive environment for sustaining health behaviors. They conclude there is a need for digital health platforms to broaden their focus beyond single domains.
limitations: The authors state that the observational design cannot establish the temporal sequence of changes, and that an experimental design is needed to test causality. They note that the single-item impact measure has yet to be validated, that industry sector and implementation factors were not examined, and that completers were more often White, which limits generalizability. Future studies should use an experimental design and longer follow-up of 6 or 12 months.

limitations.q: This study was observational in nature, meaning that while we were able to observe that depression symptoms and MVPA improved over time, we were unable to determine the temporal sequence of the changes.
A prospective, experimental design and random assignment to treatment conditions is needed to test the directionality and causality of these improvements.

abstract_claims.q: Approximately 47% of participants were physically underactive at baseline, defined as <150 min of physical activity per week.
Men participated in more physical activity than women ( _p_ = 0.005), while women and individuals identifying as gender non-binary reported more depression symptoms than men ( _p_ s < 0.05).
Older adults reported fewer depression symptoms than younger adults ( _r_ = −0.16, _p_ < 0.001).
Baseline MVPA baseline was negatively correlated with depression symptoms ( _r_ = −0.19, _p_ < 0.001).

Depression scores significantly improved, with 66.9% of adults at risk of depression improving or recovering ( _p_ < 0.001) and 94% of adults with low depression symptoms maintaining this status over time ( _p_ = 0.004).

Physical activity participation improved by 117% among individuals deemed underactive at baseline ( _p_ < 0.001), while individuals who were active at baseline maintained high levels of physical activity ( _p_ = 0.06).
Adults with access to a multi-modal digital mental health platform reported significant beneficial changes in depression symptoms and physical activity participation.
Digital mental health tools may have the potential to elicit positive change in physical health domains, as well as mental health.
